name: John Bates Jr.'s Auction Room
aka: the wooden auction-room on Dearborn Street

placement.symbolic_location: West side of Dearborn Street between Lake Street and South Water Street, fronting east onto Dearborn; placed at the middle of that block face, which the source does not state.

stories.note: Not stated. Andreas calls it 'a wooden structure ... for an auction-room' — a purpose-built single-use room rather than a store with living quarters over it — and a single-storey hall is what that describes. Two storeys is possible if Bates let the upper floor, and nothing reached says either way.

construction.note: Andreas says 'wooden' and no more, which distinguishes it from brick or stone and from nothing else. Frame rather than log because a clear-span room is what frame construction is for and log is not, and because the dossier records the town's 1833-34 stock as frame and log with new commercial work going up in frame. Braced rather than balloon frame for the reason the Sauganash record gives: the sources never use a word that separates them.

wall_height_m.note: No figure is attested. 3.6 m is about 12 ft: a single storey built taller than a dwelling's, which is what a room full of standing bidders and stacked lots needs. The reasoning is from the use, not from a measurement, and it is deliberately not the 2.5 m this project gives single-storey log dwellings.

roof_type.note: Not attested. Gable is the near-universal roof form for frame buildings of this type, period and region, and the simplest way to roof a clear-span room.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested for this building. 33 degrees is the frame_storefront archetype's own figure for a store, and it is adopted here rather than the 38 this project uses for taverns because the archetype argues the case from the dataset's one attested store footprint: a store's frontage is long and its plan shallow, so a tavern's pitch puts more roof above the eave than there is wall below it and the building stops reading as a shop. Inferred from construction practice and from the type, not measured.

chimneys.note: Not attested. One stove flue is the minimum for a room used through Chicago winters. The COUNT is the inference; the stack's position, size and material are the archetype's, per docs/LIBERTIES.md L26.

shopfront.note: An auction room is entered, not shopped in: goods were cried inside to a standing crowd rather than displayed to the street. Andreas describes the building's purpose and never its face. Inferred from the attested use; the archetype's default is a composed shopfront and turning it off is a claim this record makes deliberately.

function.note: Andreas states the purpose in the same sentence as the construction: erected 'for an auction-room'. This is one of the few buildings in this parcel whose use is documented as the reason it was built rather than inferred from its occupant's trade.

occupants.value: John Bates Jr., auctioneer and deputy postmaster
occupants.note: Andreas names Bates as the builder and the auctioneer. He was also deputy postmaster from 1833, sorting mail in Hogan's store at the other end of the town's business street — the two buildings are 570 m apart in this model and the same man worked in both.

citations.citation: Andreas, A. T. History of Chicago: From the Earliest Period to the Present Time. Vol. 1. Chicago: A. T. Andreas, 1884.
OpenStreetMap contributors. Street centerline intersection nodes for downtown Chicago, retrieved via the Overpass API, 2026-08-09.

research_note: A BUILDING WHOSE PURPOSE IS DOCUMENTED AND WHOSE EVERY DIMENSION IS INVENTED. Andreas gives the material ('a wooden structure'), the purpose ('for an auction-room'), the builder and a two-year window for the erection, and gives the location as a block face rather than a corner. The position note above is the important part of this record: the uncertainty is anisotropic — about 20 m across Dearborn Street and about 55 m along it — and the record is placed at the middle of the face purely for want of a statement. THE COLLISION WITH MADORE BEAUBIEN'S LOT IS THE THING TO WATCH. Andreas separately calls Madore Beaubien's two-roomed log house 'the first building on lot No. 1' at the south-west corner of South Water and Dearborn, which is the north end of this very block face. Both records cannot be right about everything if the auction room stood at that end. WHAT WOULD UPGRADE THIS RECORD: an 1834-35 Chicago Democrat advertisement giving Bates's sale-room address in relation to a cross street; the school-section sale notices; or the 1834 town lot records for the Dearborn frontage between Lake and South Water. See docs/RESEARCH/bates_auction_room.md.
